p: What is a verbal?
c: A verb form used as a noun, adjective, or adverb
A word that is spoken out loud
e: Gerunds, participles, and infinitives are verbals. They come from verbs but do the job of another part of speech.

p: In "Swimming is my favorite sport," what kind of verbal is "Swimming"?
e: "Swimming" ends in -ing and acts as a noun (the subject), so it is a gerund.

p: In "The barking dog woke the baby," what kind of verbal is "barking"?
e: "Barking" describes the dog, so it acts as an adjective. A verbal used as an adjective is a participle.

p: In "She wants to ski at Vail," what kind of verbal is "to ski"?
e: "To" plus the base form of a verb ("ski") makes an infinitive.

p: A gerund always acts as what part of speech?
e: A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun, as in "Skiing is fun."

p: A participle acts as what part of speech?
e: A participle describes a noun, like "the frozen lake" or "the barking dog," so it acts as an adjective.

p: How is an infinitive formed?
c: "to" plus the base form of a verb
a helping verb plus a noun
e: Examples of infinitives: to run, to ski, to win.

p: Which sentence contains a gerund?
e: "Reading" is the subject of the sentence, so it is an -ing word used as a noun: a gerund.

p: Which sentence contains a participle used as an adjective?
e: "Frozen" describes the lake, so it is a participle. In "We skated yesterday," "skated" is the main verb.

p: Which sentence contains an infinitive?
c: To win the game, we need teamwork.
e: "To win" is "to" plus a verb, so it is an infinitive.

p: In "I enjoy hiking in the Rockies," how is "hiking" used?
c: As a noun (it is what I enjoy)
e: "Hiking" names the thing I enjoy, so it is a gerund acting as a noun.

p: In "The broken window let in cold air," what is "broken"?
e: "Broken" describes the window, and it is the past participle of "break."

p: In "Her goal is to finish the marathon," what is "to finish the marathon"?
e: It starts with "to" plus the verb "finish," so it is an infinitive phrase.

p: In "Running down the hill, Leo tripped," what is "Running down the hill"?
e: The phrase describes Leo, so it acts as an adjective. That makes it a participial phrase.

p: In "Building sandcastles takes patience," what is "Building sandcastles"?
e: The phrase is the subject of the sentence, so it acts as a noun. That makes it a gerund phrase.

p: In "The kids went to the beach," why is "to the beach" not an infinitive?
c: "Beach" is a noun, so "to the beach" is a prepositional phrase
e: An infinitive is "to" plus a verb. "To the beach" is "to" plus a noun, which makes it a prepositional phrase.

p: In "The dog loves to fetch," what job does the infinitive "to fetch" do?
c: noun (it names what the dog loves)
e: "To fetch" names the thing the dog loves, so it acts as a noun.

p: In "We need a place to rest," what job does "to rest" do?
e: "To rest" tells what kind of place, so it acts as an adjective.

p: In "The rescued puppy wagged its tail," what is "rescued"?
e: "Rescued" describes the puppy, so it is a participle acting as an adjective.

p: In "My brother hates waking up early," how is "waking up early" used?
e: The phrase names what my brother hates, so it is a gerund phrase acting as a noun.

p: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
c: The ball was kicked by Sofia.
e: In the passive voice, the subject (the ball) receives the action. The verb uses a form of "be" plus a past participle: "was kicked."

p: Which sentence is in the active voice?
c: The gold was guarded by the dragon.
The gold had been guarded for years.
e: In the active voice, the subject does the action. The dragon does the guarding.

p: In the active voice, what does the subject do?
e: Active voice: "Maya threw the ball." Maya, the subject, does the throwing.

p: In the passive voice, what does the subject do?
e: Passive voice: "The ball was thrown by Maya." The ball, the subject, receives the action.

p: Which sentence rewrites "The cake was eaten by the cat" in the active voice?
c: The cat was eating by the cake.
e: In the active voice, the doer (the cat) becomes the subject: "The cat ate the cake."

p: Which sentence rewrites "Mom painted the fence" in the passive voice?
c: The fence was painted by Mom.
Mom was painted by the fence.
e: In the passive voice, the receiver (the fence) becomes the subject: "The fence was painted by Mom."

p: Why might a writer use the passive voice in "The window was broken last night"?
c: The writer does not know or does not want to say who broke it
To turn the sentence into a question
To show that it will happen in the future
Because windows always need the passive voice
e: The passive voice lets a writer focus on the action and leave out who did it.

p: Which verb is in the passive voice?
e: "Was chosen" is a form of "be" plus a past participle, which makes it passive.

p: In "The trail was cleared by volunteers," who did the action?
e: In a passive sentence, the doer often comes after "by." The volunteers cleared the trail.

p: Which sentence about the Constitution is in the passive voice?
e: "Was signed" is passive. The subject (the Constitution) receives the action.

p: Which sentence puts the focus on what received the action, not on who did it?
c: The new library was opened in June.
The mayor opened the new library in June.
The mayor will open the new library in June.
The mayor opens a new library every June.
e: The passive voice ("was opened") puts the library first and does not name who opened it.

p: Which active sentence means the same as "The goal was scored by Emma"?
e: Make the doer (Emma) the subject: "Emma scored the goal."

p: Choose the passive verb that completes the sentence: "The trophy ___ to the winning team."
e: The trophy receives the action, so the verb is passive: "was given."

p: Why do writers often choose the active voice?
c: It makes clear who is doing the action
It hides who did the action
It turns a statement into a question
e: Active sentences name the doer first, which usually makes them clear and direct.

p: What mood is the verb in? "Close the door, please."
e: A command or request uses the imperative mood.

p: What mood is the verb in? "The snow is deep today."
e: A plain statement of fact uses the indicative mood.

p: In "If I were a dragon, I would fly to school," which word is in the subjunctive mood?
e: "Were" describes something that is not true (I am not a dragon). That is the subjunctive mood.

p: What mood is the verb in? "Did you finish your homework?"
e: A question uses the interrogative mood.

p: In "We would go skiing if the lifts were open," what mood does "would go" show?
e: "Would go" tells what would happen under a condition, so it is the conditional mood.

p: Choose the verb for formal written English (subjunctive mood): "I wish I ___ taller."
e: Wishes take the subjunctive "were": "I wish I were taller."

p: Choose the subjunctive verb: "The coach insists that every player ___ on time."
e: After words like "insists that," the subjunctive uses the base form of the verb: "be."

p: Choose the subjunctive verb: "It is important that she ___ her helmet."
e: After "It is important that," the subjunctive uses the base form of the verb: "wear."

p: Which sentence is in the subjunctive mood?
c: If I were you, I would study.
e: "If I were you" describes something that is not true, which uses the subjunctive mood.

p: Which mood is used to give a command or make a request?
e: Commands like "Grab your skis" use the imperative mood.

p: Which mood is used to state a fact or an opinion?
e: Statements like "The lake is cold" use the indicative mood.

p: What is the subjunctive mood used for?
c: Wishes and situations that are not true
e: Example: "If I were a bird, I would fly." The speaker is not a bird.

p: What is the subject of this imperative sentence? "Pass the salsa."
e: In a command, the subject "you" is understood: "(You) pass the salsa."

p: Which sentence uses the conditional mood?
c: We might catch the bus if we hurry.
e: "Might catch" tells what could happen under a condition (if we hurry), which is the conditional mood.

p: What mood is the verb in? "Be quiet in the library."
e: It is a command, so it uses the imperative mood.

p: Choose the verb for formal written English (subjunctive mood): "If she ___ here, she would help us."
e: She is not here, so the sentence describes something that is not true. The subjunctive form is "were."

p: Which sentence has an incorrect shift in voice?
c: Sam baked the bread, and then the dishes were washed by him.
Sam baked the bread and then washed the dishes.
Sam baked the bread, and Lily washed the dishes.
e: The sentence starts in the active voice ("Sam baked") and shifts to the passive voice ("were washed by him").

p: Which sentence has an incorrect shift in mood?
c: Read the directions, and then you should answer the questions.
Read the directions, and then answer the questions.
You should read the directions and then answer the questions.
She read the directions and answered the questions.
e: It starts as a command (imperative) and shifts to "you should" (a statement). Keep one mood: "Read the directions, and then answer the questions."

p: How do you fix the shift in mood? "If I were older and I was taller, I would play basketball."
e: Both parts describe things that are not true, so both take the subjunctive "were": "If I were older and I were taller."

p: Which revision fixes the shift in voice? "Lena wrote the song, and it was sung by her at the show."
c: Lena wrote the song and sang it at the show.
The song was written by Lena, and she sang it at the show.
Lena wrote the song, and it was sung.
The song wrote Lena and sang at the show.
e: The fix keeps both verbs in the active voice: "wrote" and "sang."

p: Which sentence stays in the same mood the whole way through?
c: Grab your skis and meet me at the lift.
Grab your skis, and then you should meet me at the lift.
Grab your skis, and then you can meet me at the lift.
Grab your skis, and then you will meet me at the lift.
e: "Grab" and "meet" are both commands, so the whole sentence stays in the imperative mood.

p: What can an ellipsis (...) show in a quotation?
c: That some words were left out
That the sentence is a question
e: An ellipsis marks words that were left out of a quotation.

p: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show a pause?
c: Well... I guess we can go.
Well, I guess we can go.
Well; I guess we can go.
Well: I guess we can go.
e: The three dots in "Well..." show the speaker pausing.

p: Which sentence uses a dash to show a sudden break in thought?
c: I was going to call you—wait, is that a moose?
I was going to call you, wait is that a moose.
I was going to call you; wait is that a moose.
I was going to call you: wait is that a moose.
e: A dash shows a sudden break or interruption in a sentence.

p: The coach said, "Practice starts at noon, and everyone must bring water." Which shortened quotation shows the left-out words correctly?
c: "Practice starts at noon ... everyone must bring water."
"Practice starts at noon, everyone must bring water."
"Practice starts at noon? Everyone must bring water."
"Practice starts at noon; everyone must bring water."
e: The word "and" was left out, so an ellipsis (...) marks where it was.

p: Which punctuation mark shows that words were left out of a quotation?
e: An ellipsis is three dots that mark an omission (words left out).

p: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
c: My cousin, however, forgot her skis.
My cousin however, forgot her skis.
My, cousin however forgot her skis.
My cousin however forgot her, skis.
e: "However" interrupts the sentence, so it gets a comma on both sides to mark the pause.

p: Which sentence uses dashes correctly?
c: The prize—a brand-new snowboard—went to Kai.
The—prize a brand-new snowboard—went to Kai.
The prize a—brand-new snowboard went—to Kai.
The prize a brand-new—snowboard went to Kai—.
e: The dashes go around the break in the sentence: "a brand-new snowboard."

p: Find the sentence that shifts from active to passive voice partway through.
c: Ava opened the gate, and the horses were led out by her.
Ava opened the gate and led the horses out.
The gate was opened, and the horses were led out.
Ava opened the gate, and Ben led the horses out.
e: "Ava opened" is active, but "were led out by her" is passive. The same doer should stay the subject.

p: Which set of directions incorrectly shifts between moods?
c: Preheat the oven, and then you will mix the flour and sugar.
Preheat the oven, and then mix the flour and sugar.
First, preheat the oven. Next, mix the flour and sugar.
Preheat the oven and mix the flour and sugar.
e: It starts as a command (imperative) and shifts to a statement (indicative): "you will mix."

p: Which revision fixes the shift in voice? "The posters were made by the club, and they hung them in the hall."
c: The club made the posters and hung them in the hall.
The posters were made, and they hung them in the hall.
The club made the posters, and the hall was where they were hung by them.
e: Both verbs, "made" and "hung," are now in the active voice with the club as the doer.

p: Which sentence keeps the subjunctive mood the whole way through?
c: If I were the coach and he were the captain, we would win.
If I were the coach and he was the captain, we would win.
If I was the coach and he were the captain, we would win.
e: Both "if" parts describe things that are not true, so both take the subjunctive "were."

p: What kind of shift appears in this sentence? "First, measure the board, and then you cut it in half."
c: a shift in mood (imperative to indicative)
a shift in voice (active to passive)
a shift in tense (past to future)
e: "Measure the board" is a command, but "you cut it" is a statement. The fix: "measure the board, and then cut it in half."

p: What kind of shift appears in this sentence? "Jada painted the mural, and the frame was built by her too."
c: a shift from active to passive voice
a shift from imperative to indicative mood
a shift from passive to active voice
e: "Jada painted" is active, and "was built by her" is passive.

p: Which sentence avoids a shift in voice?
c: Marco fixed the bike and rode it to school.
Marco fixed the bike, and it was ridden to school by him.
The bike was fixed by Marco, and he rode it to school.
Marco fixed the bike, and then the bike was ridden by him.
e: "Fixed" and "rode" are both active, with Marco as the doer.

p: Choose the verb that keeps the mood consistent: "The librarian requested that we be quiet and that we ___ the books on the cart."
e: After "requested that," both verbs use the subjunctive base form: "be" and "leave."

p: Which revision fixes the mood shift? "Wear sunscreen, and you should also bring a hat."
c: Wear sunscreen, and also bring a hat.
Wear sunscreen, and a hat should also be brought.
Wear sunscreen, and you will also bring a hat.
e: Both parts are now commands, so the sentence stays in the imperative mood.

p: Why is this sentence awkward? "We cleaned the campsite, and the fire was put out by us."
c: It shifts from active to passive voice.
It shifts from the imperative to the subjunctive mood.
e: "We cleaned" is active, but "was put out by us" is passive. Better: "We cleaned the campsite and put out the fire."

p: Which sentence correctly uses commas around the phrase that renames "Mr. Ruiz"?
c: Mr. Ruiz, our science teacher, loves rocks.
Mr. Ruiz our science teacher, loves rocks.
Mr. Ruiz our science teacher loves, rocks.
Mr. Ruiz our, science teacher loves rocks.
e: "Our science teacher" renames Mr. Ruiz, so it needs a comma on both sides.

p: Which sentence uses a dash to set off an important idea at the end?
c: We packed everything for the trip—except the tent.
We packed everything for the trip except—the tent.
We—packed everything for the trip except the tent.
We packed everything—for the trip except the tent.
e: The dash creates a break right before the surprise detail: "except the tent."

p: In "I think... no, I know I left it here," what does the ellipsis show?
c: The speaker pauses before changing course
e: In dialogue, an ellipsis can show a pause or hesitation.

p: A speaker is cut off in the middle of a sentence. Which ending shows this best?
e: A dash at the end of dialogue shows that the speaker was suddenly interrupted.

p: In dialogue, how is a dash different from an ellipsis?
c: A dash shows a sudden break; an ellipsis shows a trailing off or hesitation
A dash shows a question; an ellipsis shows a command
A dash ends every sentence; an ellipsis starts every sentence
e: A dash cuts off sharply. An ellipsis fades out or pauses.

p: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory word?
e: An introductory word like "Yes" is followed by a comma to mark the pause.

p: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off extra information?
c: Pikes Peak, which is over 14,000 feet tall, is near Colorado Springs.
Pikes Peak which is over 14,000 feet tall, is near Colorado Springs.
Pikes Peak, which is over 14,000 feet tall is near Colorado Springs.
Pikes Peak which, is over 14,000 feet tall is near Colorado Springs.
e: The extra detail "which is over 14,000 feet tall" needs a comma on both sides.

p: Which sentence uses a dash to create a dramatic pause before a surprise?
c: I opened the box and found—a puppy!
I opened—the box and found a puppy!
I—opened the box and found a puppy!
I opened the box—and found a puppy—!
e: The dash makes the reader pause right before the surprise: "a puppy!"

p: A sign reads: "Our town park has a pond, a playground, and a skate ramp." Which quotation correctly leaves out "a playground"?
c: "Our town park has a pond ... and a skate ramp."
"Our town park has a pond and a skate ramp."
"Our town park has a pond, a playground ... and a skate ramp."
e: The ellipsis shows exactly where "a playground" was removed. Without it, the quotation is not exact.

p: When you shorten a quotation with an ellipsis, what rule must you follow?
c: Leaving words out must not change the speaker's meaning
You must leave out at least half the words
You must turn the quotation into a question
You can use an ellipsis only once per page
e: An ellipsis is honest only if the shortened quotation still means what the speaker meant.

p: The principal said, "I do not think we should cancel the game." Which shortened quotation changes the principal's meaning?
c: "I ... think we should cancel the game."
"I do not think we should cancel the game."
The principal does not think "we should cancel the game."
e: Leaving out "do not" flips the meaning. That is a misuse of the ellipsis.

p: How many dots are in a standard ellipsis?
e: An ellipsis is three dots: ...

p: Which quotation of "The trail, which is steep and rocky, leads to the lake" correctly uses an ellipsis?
c: "The trail ... which is steep and rocky, leads to the lake."
"The trail, which is steep and rocky ... leads ... to the lake."
e: The ellipsis replaces the left-out words "which is steep and rocky." The other choices leave words out with no mark or add dots where nothing was removed.

p: Choose the correct spelling of the word that means "to get."
e: After the letter c, use "ei": receive.

p: Choose the correct spelling of the word that means "needed."
e: "Necessary" has one c and two s's.

p: Add -ing to "begin." Which spelling is correct?
e: "Begin" is stressed on the last syllable and ends in one vowel plus one consonant, so double the n: beginning.

p: Add -ed to "occur." Which spelling is correct?
e: "Occur" is stressed on the last syllable and ends in one vowel plus one consonant, so double the r: occurred.

p: Which sentence spells "separate" correctly?
c: Keep the eggs separate from the flour.
Keep the eggs seperate from the flour.
Keep the eggs seperete from the flour.
Keep the eggs separete from the flour.
e: The correct spelling is "separate." There is "a rat" in sep-a-rat-e.

p: Which word meaning "for sure" is spelled correctly?
e: "Definitely" comes from "definite," so it is spelled with an i, not an a.

p: Add -ful to "beauty." Which spelling is correct?
e: When a word ends in a consonant plus y, change the y to i before adding -ful. The suffix -ful has one l.

p: A mystery writer wants to keep the thief's identity secret. Which sentence works best?
c: The diamond was stolen during the party.
The butler stole the diamond during the party.
The butler is stealing the diamond.
Did the butler steal the diamond?
e: The passive voice ("was stolen") lets the writer leave out who did it.

p: A coach wants to sound direct and urgent. Which sentence does that best?
c: Run to the fence and back!
It would be nice if you ran to the fence and back.
Maybe you could run to the fence and back.
Running to the fence and back was done.
e: The imperative mood gives a direct command, which sounds urgent.

p: Why might a poet write "If I were the wind, I would carry you home"?
c: The subjunctive mood shows an imagined, wished-for situation
The imperative mood gives a direct command
The passive voice hides who did the action
The indicative mood states a proven fact
e: The speaker is not the wind. "If I were" shows an imagined situation.

p: A news reporter writes, "Three hikers were rescued by firefighters." Why might the reporter use the passive voice here?
c: To put the focus on the hikers, who are the main part of the story
To give a command to the reader
To show the event has not happened yet
To ask the reader a question
e: The passive voice puts the receiver of the action (the hikers) first.

p: Which sentence uses the active voice to make clear who is responsible?
c: Mistakes were made with the library book.
The library book has been lost.
e: In "I lost the library book," the doer is named as the subject. The other sentences hide who did it.

p: Which sentence keeps the focus on the step in an experiment, not on the person doing it?
c: The water was heated to 100 degrees Celsius.
I heated the water to 100 degrees Celsius.
Heat the water to 100 degrees Celsius!
Would you heat the water to 100 degrees Celsius?
e: The passive voice puts the water and the step first and leaves out the person.

p: Use context clues: "The trail was so arduous that even the strongest hikers needed many breaks." What does "arduous" mean?
e: Even strong hikers needed breaks, so the trail was hard.

p: Use context clues: "Unlike his gregarious sister, who loves parties, Theo is quiet and shy." What does "gregarious" mean?
e: "Unlike" signals a contrast with "quiet and shy," and she loves parties, so she is outgoing.

p: Use context clues: "Food was scarce; there was barely enough for one person." What does "scarce" mean?
e: "Barely enough" tells you there was not much food.

p: Use context clues: "After the long drought, the farmers welcomed the rain that finally fell." What does "drought" mean?
e: The farmers were glad the rain "finally" came, so it had been dry for a long time.

p: Use context clues: "The puppy was so docile that it let the kids pick it up, brush it, and dress it in a sweater." What does "docile" mean?
e: The puppy let the kids do all those things, so it was calm and easy to handle.

p: Use context clues: "Maria was elated, jumping up and down when she heard she made the team." What does "elated" mean?
e: Jumping up and down after good news shows great happiness.

p: In "A meteorologist, a scientist who studies weather, gave the forecast," what kind of context clue explains "meteorologist"?
c: a definition set off by commas
e: The phrase between the commas tells exactly what a meteorologist is.

p: Use context clues: "The ancient map was so fragile that it tore when Ava barely touched it." What does "fragile" mean?
e: It tore at a light touch, so it breaks easily. "Ancient" is what tells you it is old.

p: The Greek root "bio" (as in "biology" and "biography") means:
e: Biology is the study of life. A biography is the story of a person's life.

p: The Latin root "port" in "transport" and "portable" means:
e: Something portable can be carried. To transport is to carry across.

p: The prefix "mal-" in "malfunction" means:
e: A malfunction is when something works badly.

p: The Greek root "chron" in "chronological" means:
e: Chronological order is time order.

p: The Latin root "dict" means "say or speak." Which word uses that root?
e: To dictate is to say words aloud for someone to write down.

p: The suffix "-ology" (as in "geology") means:
e: Geology is the study of the earth.

p: The Latin root "rupt" (as in "erupt" and "interrupt") means:
e: A volcano erupts when lava bursts out. To interrupt is to break into a conversation.

p: "Tele" means far and "scope" means look at. What is a telescope?
c: a tool for looking at faraway things
e: Put the parts together: a tool for looking at things that are far away.

p: The prefix "anti-" in "antibacterial" means:
e: Antibacterial soap works against bacteria.

p: Which reference would best help you find a synonym for "happy"?
e: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings (synonyms).

p: In a dictionary entry, what does the label "n." tell you?
e: "n." stands for noun, which is the word's part of speech.

p: Which part of a dictionary entry tells you whether a word comes from Latin or Greek?
e: The etymology gives the history and origin of a word.

p: The guide words at the top of a dictionary page are "plant" and "pluck." Which word would be on that page?
e: In alphabetical order, "plate" comes after "plant" and before "pluck."

p: Which is an example of verbal irony?
c: Stepping into a cold rainstorm, Jay said, "What lovely weather!"
Jay said, "It is raining, so I brought an umbrella."
The rain fell like a curtain.
The rain whispered on the roof.
e: Jay says the opposite of what he means. The weather is not lovely.

p: What is verbal irony?
c: Saying the opposite of what you really mean
Giving human traits to an object
e: Example: calling a muddy, freezing day "perfect beach weather."

p: Which sentence contains a pun?
c: I used to be a baker, but I could not make enough dough.
The bakery opens at six in the morning.
The bread was as hard as a rock.
The oven roared like a lion.
e: "Dough" means both bread dough and money. That double meaning makes a pun.

p: What is a pun?
c: A joke that plays on a word with two meanings or a sound-alike word
A word that imitates a sound
e: Example: "The math book looked sad because it had too many problems."

p: Explain the pun: "The skeleton did not go to the dance because he had no body to go with."
c: "No body" sounds like "nobody," and a skeleton has no body
"Dance" means both a party and a song
"Skeleton" means both bones and a plan
e: The joke works because "no body" and "nobody" sound the same.

p: After Zoe tripped and spilled her lunch tray, her brother said, "Smooth move." What kind of language is this?
e: The move was clumsy, not smooth. Saying the opposite of what you mean is verbal irony.

p: Which words create the pun in "I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. It's impossible to put down"?
e: "Put down" means to stop reading a book. It also means to set something down, which anti-gravity would make impossible.

p: Complete the analogy: hot is to cold as tall is to ___.
e: Hot and cold are opposites, so the answer is the opposite of tall.

p: Complete the analogy: author is to book as composer is to ___.
e: An author creates a book, and a composer creates a song.

p: Complete the analogy: petal is to flower as page is to ___.
e: A petal is part of a flower, and a page is part of a book.

p: Which pair shows the same relationship as "puppy : dog"?
e: A puppy is a young dog, and a kitten is a young cat.

p: Which word does NOT belong with "rapid, swift, quick"?
e: The other words mean fast. "Sluggish" means slow.

p: Which word for someone careful with money has the most positive connotation?
e: "Thrifty" sounds wise. The others suggest the person will not share.

p: Which word for someone who wants to know things has the most negative connotation?
e: "Nosy" suggests prying into other people's business.

p: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
c: Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling a word carries
Denotation is the feeling a word carries; connotation is the dictionary meaning
Denotation is a word's spelling; connotation is its sound
e: "Home" and "house" have similar denotations, but "home" has a warmer connotation.

p: "Childish" and "youthful" both describe being like a young person. How are they different?
c: "Youthful" is a noun, and "childish" is a verb
e: "Childish" suggests acting immature. "Youthful" suggests energy and freshness.

p: An ad calls a tiny house "cozy" instead of "cramped." Why?
e: Both words can describe a small space, but "cozy" makes it sound warm and inviting.

p: Which word gives the most positive feeling about a person who keeps trying?
e: "Determined" sounds admirable. The others suggest refusing to listen.

p: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
c: Walking to school, the rain started to fall.
Walking to school, I felt the rain start to fall.
As I walked to school, the rain started to fall.
The rain started to fall while I walked to school.
e: The rain was not walking to school. The person who was walking is never named.

p: Which sentence has the modifier in the right place?
c: We gave the dog with the spotted tail a bone.
We gave the dog a bone with the spotted tail.
With the spotted tail, we gave the dog a bone.
We gave with the spotted tail the dog a bone.
e: "With the spotted tail" should sit right next to "the dog," the word it describes.

p: "I saw a moose hiking up the trail." Which revision makes clear that I was the one hiking?
c: While I was hiking up the trail, I saw a moose.
I saw a moose that was hiking up the trail.
Hiking up the trail, a moose was seen.
I saw, hiking up the trail, a moose.
e: Naming "I" in the clause "While I was hiking" removes the confusion.

p: Which sentence has parallel structure?
c: I like skiing, hiking, and swimming.
I like skiing, hiking, and to swim.
I like to ski, hiking, and swimming.
I like skiing, to hike, and swim.
e: All three items use the same form: skiing, hiking, swimming.

p: Which revision makes the list parallel? "The coach told us to stretch, drink water, and that we should rest."
c: The coach told us to stretch, drink water, and rest.
The coach told us stretching, drink water, and that we should rest.
The coach told us to stretch, drinking water, and rest.
e: All three items are now base verbs after "to": stretch, drink, rest.

p: Which sentence is NOT parallel?
c: Our dog is friendly, loyal, and likes to play fetch.
Our dog is friendly, loyal, and playful.
Our dog likes to run, to swim, and to play fetch.
Our dog runs, swims, and plays fetch.
e: "Friendly" and "loyal" are adjectives, but "likes to play fetch" is a verb phrase. Fix: "friendly, loyal, and playful."

p: Choose the correct verb: "Each of the players ___ a water bottle."
e: The subject is "Each," which is singular. "Of the players" does not change that.

p: Choose the correct verb: "Neither the coach nor the players ___ ready."
e: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the closer subject. "Players" is plural, so use "are."

p: Choose the correct verb: "The box of crayons ___ on the shelf."
e: The subject is "box," which is singular. "Of crayons" is just a describing phrase.

p: Choose the pronoun that agrees: "Both of my brothers lost ___ mittens."
e: "Both" is plural, so the pronoun is "their."

p: Choose the correct pronoun: "The tree dropped ___ leaves."
e: "Tree" is singular and not a person, so use "its." "It's" means "it is."

p: Which sentence has a pronoun with an unclear antecedent?
c: When Maya talked to Ella, she was upset.
When Maya talked to Ella, Maya was upset.
Maya was upset when she talked to Ella.
Ella was upset when Maya talked to her.
e: "She" could mean Maya or Ella, so the reader cannot tell who was upset.

p: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
c: The lift closed early; the wind was too strong.
The lift closed early; because the wind was too strong.
The lift; closed early because the wind was too strong.
The lift closed; early because the wind was too strong.
e: A semicolon joins two complete sentences that are closely related.

p: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
c: Bring three things: a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
Bring: a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
Bring three things a hat: gloves, and a scarf.
Bring three: things a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
e: A colon comes after a complete thought ("Bring three things") to introduce a list.

p: Which sentence uses semicolons correctly in a list?
c: We visited Denver, Colorado; Salt Lake City, Utah; and Boise, Idaho.
We visited Denver; Colorado, Salt Lake City; Utah, and Boise; Idaho.
We visited; Denver, Colorado, Salt Lake City, Utah, and Boise, Idaho.
e: When list items already have commas, semicolons separate the items.

p: Choose the correct word: "The new rule had a big ___ on recess."
e: "Effect" is usually a noun meaning a result. "Affect" is usually a verb.

p: Choose the correct word: "___ going to the game after school."
e: "They're" is short for "they are": "They are going to the game."

p: Choose the correct word: "My little sister is already taller ___ me."
e: Use "than" to compare. "Then" is about time.

p: Which sentence is a comma splice?
c: The game ended, we went home.
The game ended, and we went home.
The game ended; we went home.
When the game ended, we went home.
e: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

p: Which revision fixes the comma splice? "I love snow, it makes everything quiet."
c: I love snow because it makes everything quiet.
I love snow it makes everything quiet.
I love snow, it makes, everything quiet.
I love, snow it makes everything quiet.
e: Adding "because" turns the second part into a dependent clause, so the comma splice is gone.
